evals.name: jaggies-on-android
evals.prompt: My three.js game looks smooth on my laptop but a player sent an Android screenshot where every edge is jagged and the outlines look dashed. I already pass antialias: true to WebGLRenderer. Can you fix it?
evals.expected_output: Diagnoses which profile/context drew the screenshot before changing anything, finds the cause (MSAA off or ignored, or a DPR-1 canvas upscaled by the phone), and fixes it with MSAA rather than a post-process AA pass, proven by a reported aa value and a device screenshot.
assertions: Before proposing a fix, it determines which quality profile / context the phone actually used, rather than assuming the desktop path.
It checks real anti-aliasing via gl.getParameter(gl.SAMPLES) (or a health hook reporting it), not only the antialias flag passed to the constructor or getContextAttributes().
It compares the renderer's pixel ratio against devicePixelRatio and explains that a DPR-1 canvas upscaled by the phone produces stair-steps and dashed thin outlines.
It does not add FXAA or SMAA as the fix; it uses MSAA (or a multisampled render target if SAMPLES is 0) and says why post-process AA would blur sprites and text.
Verification includes an exposed aa / health value and a screenshot from the real device, not only a headless crop.

evals.name: fxaa-blurs-pixel-art
evals.prompt: I added an FXAA pass with EffectComposer to my WebGL pixel-art game to get rid of jaggies. Now the sprites and the score text look smeared. If I remove FXAA the edges are jagged again even though antialias is true. What should I do?
evals.expected_output: Explains that FXAA blurs pixel art and text because it works on the final image, and that EffectComposer renders into its own target so canvas antialias no longer applies; replaces FXAA with a multisampled composer render target (or direct rendering with MSAA) and checks sprite texture filtering.
assertions: It explains that post-process AA cannot tell a sprite's hard pixel edges from geometry edges, so it blurs pixel art and small text.
It identifies that EffectComposer renders the scene into its own render target, which is why antialias: true on the renderer stops affecting the scene.
The fix uses MSAA: a render target with samples (e.g. 4) passed to the composer, or rendering without the composer, rather than tuning FXAA parameters.
It mentions checking texture filtering (NearestFilter / no mipmaps for sprites) as a separate cause of blurry pixel art.
It proposes an A/B comparison crop (no AA vs candidate vs MSAA) of one edge and one text region.

evals.name: context-lost-safe-mode
evals.prompt: Some phones show a white canvas a few seconds after my three.js game loads, but the HTML score overlay keeps updating. I want a low-quality mode for weak GPUs, but I don't want those players stuck with jagged graphics.
evals.expected_output: A profile ladder (full / safe-with-MSAA / bare) chosen at boot, an early-failure self-heal that steps down one rung and reloads at most once per rung per tab via sessionStorage, an on-screen graphics banner naming the profile and GPU, and a headless proof of the heal loop with WEBGL_lose_context.
assertions: It defines at least three profiles where the low-power 'safe' profile keeps MSAA and a further 'bare' profile drops it, instead of turning MSAA off in safe mode permanently.
The self-heal steps down one profile and reloads only on an early failure, and records the profiles already healed from in sessionStorage so reloads are bounded and cannot loop.
It handles webglcontextlost with preventDefault() and reports a lost context or blank frame on screen with the profile and GPU name, instead of leaving a silent white canvas.
Storage reads and writes are wrapped in try/catch.
It proves the heal path headlessly by calling WEBGL_lose_context.loseContext() and asserting the full -> safe -> bare -> banner sequence with a bounded number of reloads.
